August 13, 2026

VIA ETARIFF
Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Esq., Secretary
Carlos Clay, Deputy Secretary
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission 
888 First Street, N.E.
Washington, DC  20426

Re:	Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, Response to Deficiency Letter, 
Docket No. ER26-2562-00_ 

Dear Secretaries:
 On July 29, 2026, the Acting Director, Division of Electric Power Regulation – East of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”) issued a letter to Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC (“DEC”) in the above-captioned dockets stating that the filings submitted in such dockets were deficient (“letter”).  In the letter, the Director requested complete responses to the questions in Section I below.  Responses are due by August 28, 2026. 
Capitalized terms used but not defined herein have the meaning ascribed to them in DEC’s Joint Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Joint OATT”).  This transmittal letter contains information required by Part 35 of the regulations of the Commission.  In the event of any inconsistencies, discrepancies, or conflicts between the language in this transmittal letter and the terms of the Joint OATT, the Joint OATT shall control.
BACKGROUND
On May 18, 2026, DEC submitted to the Commission a revised Network Integration Transmission Service Agreement between itself and Piedmont Municipal Power Agency (“PMPA”) (“PMPA NITSA”) in Docket No. ER26-2562. The PMPA NITSA is OATT Service Agreement No. 355 under Tariff Volume No. 4, DEC’s Joint Open Access Transmission Tariff.  The revisions to the PMPA NITSA were related to PMPA’s request for network integration transmission service to serve an additional 50 MW of new Network Load at a new Delivery Point No. 14 (Rock Hill) by September 30, 2028, along with other more ministerial revisions described in the transmittal letter to the filing.  DEC requested an August 1, 2026 effective date for such filing.
On May 29, 2026, DEC submitted to the Commission revisions to Attachment F-2 (Form of Service Agreement for Network Integration Transmission Service (DEC Zone)) to its Joint OATT in Docket No. ER26-2691.  DEC proposed to revise (1) the body of the pro forma NITSA, (2) the Specifications for Network Integration Transmission Service (Attachment A to the pro forma NITSA), and (3) other attachments to the pro forma NITSA as described in the transmittal letter to the filing.  DEC requested an August 1, 2026 effective date for such filing.
RESPONSE TO COMMISSION QUESTIONS
DEC responds to the Acting Director’s questions in the letter below (internal citations omitted). 
In DEC’s pro forma NITSA transmittal, DEC states that:  
if the costs of network upgrades necessary to accommodate network service to a network customer are rolled into Transmission Provider’s transmission rates under Attachment H of the Joint OATT and if such customer subsequently makes a payment to Transmission Provider as a result of a Transmission Customer Shortfall Event, then Transmission Provider will appropriately reflect the customer’s payment in its transmission cost of service pursuant to Attachment H to the Joint OATT.
Please confirm whether any portion of a shortfall payment made under Attachment F is also recovered through transmission rates under section 6.6.3 of Attachment A, and, if so, identify the tariff provision that prevents double recovery.
Response:  DEC is not seeking to double recover the amount of a shortfall payment from both (1) wholesale transmission customers paying wholesale transmission formula rates and (2) the individual NITS customer responsible per its NITSA for payment of the shortfall payment amount.  Rather, DEC is seeking to recover the shortfall payment only from the individual NITS customer responsible per the terms and conditions of its NITSA for such payment.  To this end, DEC structured Section 5 of Section II of Attachment F of the pro forma NITSA to prevent double recovery by providing for a direct charging mechanism via an invoice to be sent by the Transmission Provider to only the NITS customer responsible for payment of the shortfall amount per the terms of its individual NITSA.
Sections 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3 of Section II of Attachment F of the proposed pro forma NITSA explain how the shortfall payment is calculated which is specific to the particular NITS customer (not all wholesale transmission customers via formula rates).  The Committed Revenue Contribution calculation is explained in Section 5.1 and is specific to the particular NITS customer (not applicable to transmission customers via formula rates).  The Actual Revenue Contribution calculation is explained in Section 5.2 and is specific to the particular NITS customer (again, not applicable to transmission customers via formula rates).  The Shortfall Payment Event and Shortfall Payment Obligation are each explained in Section 5.4 and is specific to the particular NITS customer (not to transmission customers via formula rates).
Section 5.5 of Section II of Attachment F of the proposed pro forma NITSA (excerpt below) explains that an invoice for the shortfall payment amount will be issued to the Transmission Customer (not all Transmission Customers, only the particular customer under its particular, individualized NITSA).
5.5  Timing of Payment.  Transmission Customer shall make payment of the Transmission Customer Shortfall Payment Obligation to the Transmission Provider within 20 days of receipt of an invoice to be issued by the Transmission Provider following its annual calculation of the Transmission Customer Shortfall Payment Obligation.    
The shortfall payment would not be included in DEC’s wholesale transmission formula rates as an addition to the transmission revenue requirement because the shortfall payment would be charged to a particular NITS customer (so not broadly charged to all NITS customers through transmission formula rates).  Due to the structure of Section 5 of Section II of Attachment F of the proposed pro forma NITSA, only the NITS customer to whom the shortfall payment obligation applies would be issued an invoice for such payment.  As a result, no portion of a shortfall payment made under Attachment F is also recovered through transmission rates.  
To the extent a shortfall payment is credited to formula rates, describe how and when it is reflected through Attachment H. 
Response: With respect to how a shortfall payment would be credited to the transmission revenue requirement, any shortfall payment paid by the obligated NITS customer would be credited to FERC Account No. 456.  FERC Account No. 456 is a revenue account, not an expense account, and within the transmission formula rate, balances in Account No. 456 are credited to the transmission revenue requirement, reducing the transmission revenue requirement which benefits all OATT formula rate customers.  FERC Account No. 456 is specifically referenced as a revenue account in the DEC formula rate template that is pending before the Commission in Docket No. ER26-3216.  The image below is a portion of the DEC formula rate template pending in the above-mentioned proceeding which shows that FERC Account No. 456 (banded by the red box) is a revenue account included in total revenue credits (banded by the green box) which reduces the transmission revenue requirement.


The image below is a portion of the DEC formula rate template pending in the above-mentioned proceeding which is the template to be used to include amounts in FERC Account No. 456, containing the following columns to be populated: 
(a) Description -- a description of the payment, 
(b) Amount -- the amount of the payment, 
(c) Allocation Type -- the allocation type to be used, 
(d) Allocation Factor -- the transmission plant allocation factor to be used, and 
(e) OATT Amount -- the total amount of the payment that will be included in Account No. 456 as part of the Revenue Credits.
 
With respect to when a shortfall payment would be credited to the transmission revenue requirement, the formula rate update process occurs on an annual basis, commencing in May of each year utilizing the prior calendar year FERC Form No. 1 data to populate the formula rate.  A revenue credit for a shortfall payment will be reflected in the transmission formula rate that is based on the FERC Form No. 1 for the year during which the shortfall payment occurred. 
For illustration purposes, if an individual NITS customer made a shortfall payment which was received by DEC in 2028, DEC would include such amount in FERC Account No. 456, and DEC would identify such amount in DEC’s 2028 FERC Form No. 1.  In May 2029, DEC would complete the 2029 Annual Update utilizing DEC’s 2028 FERC Form No. 1 where the balance in Account No. 456 would be incorporated into the wholesale formula rate for rates charged to customers from June 1, 2029 through May 31, 2030. 
In addition to the information provided above concerning how and when a shortfall payment would be credited to the transmission revenue requirement, it is important to note that there are no currently effective or pending DEC NITSAs with any NITS customers (including the PMPA NITSA) that contain the shortfall liability provisions which DEC has described in its transmittal letter in this proceeding as being first introduced in the proposed pro forma NITSA.  A shortfall liability situation will not arise until (a) a DEC NITS customer proposes changes to NITS involving a load 100 MW or greater, (b) DEC amends the current NITSA with such customer to fill out the bracketed information in Attachment F to the NITSA to include information about the shortfall liability provisions, (c) the revised NITSA becomes effective, (d) any Direct Assignment Facilities and Network Upgrades have been constructed if needed to accommodate such change in service request, (e) an annual assessment of a shortfall liability obligation has occurred, (f) DEC determines that a shortfall payment obligation exists, (g) DEC issues an invoice to the NITSA customer pursuant to the terms of Attachment F to the NITSA to charge the shortfall payment amount, and (h) DEC receives a payment from the customer of such amount.  All of these actions would need to occur prior to a shortfall payment actually being received by DEC, which is not expected to occur until 2027 at the earliest.
Finally, DEC submits that the shortfall payment liability obligation is just and reasonable for all of the reasons set forth in the transmittal letter filed in this proceeding and that it is grounded on a well-established line of eleven separate cases in which the Commission found such obligation to likewise be just and reasonable in each and every case.  While beyond the scope of the filings submitted in these proceedings, DEC’s pending transmission formula rate update will ensure that the shortfall payment is appropriately credited against the transmission revenue requirement.  The fact that crediting of the shortfall payment is addressed within DEC’s pending transmission formula rate does not render the shortfall payment liability obligation filed in Docket No. ER26-2691 inherently unjust and unreasonable, especially considering that, as noted above, there are several conditions that must be satisfied before DEC would receive any shortfall payment.

Please explain whether the methodology, scope, or assumptions of the System Impact Study or Facilities Study will vary based on the MW size or other characteristics of the requested Network Load, including for requests of 100 MW or greater.
Response:  
DEC performs system impact studies and facilities studies for NITS customers on a fair and non-discriminatory basis utilizing the methodology, scope and assumptions described below.
Methodology:  With respect to study methodology for system impact studies, DEC follows Part C (DEC Zone) of Attachment D (Methodology for Completing a System Impact Study) to its Joint OATT which explains that DEC “will perform studies using power flow, transfer, stability, fault and other analyses as necessary and appropriate to determine whether sufficient transmission capability is available and to identify any system constraints resulting from the requested transmission service.”  Part C of Attachment D to the Joint OATT further explains that “[m]ore detailed criteria and processes utilized by the Transmission Provider in performing a System Impact Study are set forth in the Transmission Provider's annual FERC Form No. 715 submittal.”
DEC’s FERC Form No. 715 submittal describes the criteria used to perform system impact studies in Part 4 of the submittal which states that DEC uses (a) NERC’s Reliability Standards, (b) NERC’s Transmission Transfer Capability document, (c) SERC’s Regional Criteria and Reliability Standards, and (d) DEC’s Transmission System Planning Guidelines (submitted as part of the FERC Form No. 715 submission).  The planning guidelines are contained in Part V of the document and set forth the voltage and thermal guidelines to be applied when conducting studies, the selected contingencies to be utilized, and the types of studies and analyses to be performed including transformer tertiary studies, optimal power flow studies, grid voltage study for nuclear loss-of-cooling accident, stability studies (angle and voltage), power transfer studies, impact studies (power flow, transfer, stability, fault, and other analyses), fault duty studies, equipment and system loss evaluations, and facility adequacy evaluations.
DEC’s FERC Form No. 715 submittal also describes the processes utilized to perform system impact studies in Part 5 of the submittal which states that DEC uses the assessment practices promulgated by the SERC Near-Term Power Flow Working Group (including its procedural manuals).  DEC further describes that study reports, reports published by the various joint study groups in which DEC participates (i.e. SERC Long-Term Power Flow Working Group reliability studies and SERC Near-Term Power Flow Working Group operating studies) typically contain some description of the transmission planning assessment practices used and may also contain a listing of the contingencies considered.  
Scope:  With respect to study scope, DEC explains in its study reports posted on OASIS what the scope of the particular study entailed based on the particular studies and analyses performed which could include power flow, thermal, transfer, stability, short circuit/fault, power quality, and other analyses such as electromagnetic transient analyses and analyses of impacts to nearby synchronous generators (including sub-synchronous tortional interaction and sub-synchronous resonance).  For example, a recent system impact study completed by DEC describes such scope as follows in the report posted on OASIS: 
“The thermal study uses DEC Transmission Planning’s screening process to model system contingencies required in the NERC TPL-001 standard. The screening process provides branch loadings for postulated contingencies under various generation dispatches. Screenings were performed on both the base case as well as the case with the Customer’s new load applied. The results are compared to identify significant impacts to the Company Transmission System. System upgrades are identified where the Customer’s load causes a violation of the Duke Energy Transmission System Planning Guidelines, which can be found on the OASIS website. 
Short Circuit Analysis is performed using the ASPEN Breaker Rating Module. The Base Case for the short circuit analysis was developed by modifying the existing ASPEN model and implementing all the planned system upgrades as a result of the new load at the Customer’s load additions. Based on projected increases in system fault current contributions, breakers are identified using a 97% threshold of interrupting capability.   Additionally, the breakers will be included in the evaluation only if there was a greater than 3% increase compared to the rating of the existing breaker. 
If the Customer provides a dynamic load model, it will be used for stability studies. If the Customer fails to provide a dynamic load model, a generic model such as the CMLD Server Farm load model will be utilized.”
Assumptions:  With respect to study assumptions, DEC explains in its study reports posted on OASIS what assumptions were used to conduct each study.  
For system impact studies, study assumptions include the cases used in the study and any modifications to such cases.  For example, a recent system impact study completed by DEC describes such assumptions as follows in the report posted on OASIS:  
“The power flow cases used in the study were developed from the DEC internal case year 2029 (summer and winter) and 2036 (summer). The cases were modified to include new load at the Customer’s facility. The study cases were re-dispatched, solved, and saved for use.”
For facilities studies, study assumptions include assumptions related to how DEC estimates the time to complete any required Direct Assignment Facilities and Network Upgrades, as well as how DEC estimates the cost of such facilities and upgrades.  For example, a recent facilities study report posted on OASIS describes the assumptions DEC used in completing the facilities study:
“The following assumptions related to the proposed solution have been used to develop the Estimated Time to Completion and Estimated Cost: 
• The Company’s facilities described in this report are required to serve load up to 50 MW [the requested load by the customer]. 
• The Company’s facilities are based on application of Industry standard equipment. 
• The interconnection voltage at the Point of Interconnection will be a nominal value of 100kV. 
• This Facilities Study is premised on the Company providing a turnkey design and installation of all specified New Facilities for a new 100kV interconnection of the Customer. 
• The tap location is assumed to be at the location of existing structure 61 on the Robb 100kV Lines. Final tap location will be determined based on Customer obtained R/W to the existing Company transmission easement. Variation in this location may impact the scope, cost, and timeline provided in this report. 
• Temporary pullout poles will be used to facilitate the replacement of existing structure 61 under single circuit clearances. 
• Required outages can be achieved in coordination with other planned outages. 
• Material procurement is based upon current market conditions as of the date of this Report.
• The motor operation of the GOAB will be powered via a distribution delivery from the existing distribution circuit on Old Post Rd. 
• Additional Right-of-Way (R/W) will be required by the Company from the Customer. The Customer shall convey all lands required by the Company at no cost and in a manner that will not impact the project schedule. 
• All Company-proposed facilities are not located within environmentally sensitive areas such as floodplain, floodway, wetlands, contaminated sites, etc. 
• The protection schemes installed by the Company for the interconnection, including standard protection schemes, are intended to protect the Company’s Network from the Customer’s Facilities. Electrical protection schemes for the Customer’s facilities shall be the responsibility of the Customer. The Customer’s protection scheme shall be coordinated with the Company’s station protection schemes. Facilities Study Report 
• Environmental conditions will not exist that delay the construction at the site or any of the referenced work, including but not limited to wetland mitigation, floodplain impacts/studies, endangered species identification, and/or historic resources. 
• No public opposition will occur to the project, including but not limited to, the Company’s new transmission line facilities or additional required R/W. 
• Company will have the full support of necessary government agencies and regulators in expediting solutions to all permitting and regulatory issues. Permits for all work must be obtained in a manner that will not impact the project schedule. 
• Construction access to both the existing transmission line easement and future facilities must always remain free and clear of all obstructions, and meet the access requirements directed by the Company, until completion of project. 
• Adherence by Customer to Use Guidelines for Encroachments Involving Transmission Easements (a copy of which is in this report) is required. 
• Conditions will exist (including but not limited to no significant storm events, acts of God, Force Majeure, or other) during Company Construction to allow the Construction to proceed as planned. 
• Conditions will exist (including but not limited to mild temperatures, no significant storm events, acts of God, Force Majeure, or other) that will allow for the existing Bulk Electric System to be modified for purposes of installing new structures in the existing easement, physically connecting to the new infrastructure, and performing any checkout/commissioning/testing or otherwise required to complete the project. 
• All estimates prepared for this Facilities Study are considered to be good faith estimates represented in present day dollars as of the date of the study. The estimates are further premised on the Company being able to perform work during normal business hours with minimum overtime or weekend work.”
Variations by MW Size or Other Characteristics: With respect to whether system impact and facilities studies vary by MW size or other characteristics, DEC performs system impact and facilities studies for various MW sizes and other characteristics based on the same methodology as set forth above.  However, the characteristics of each NITS request drives individualized scopes and assumptions for the studies.  For the scope of the study, DEC chooses what types of studies to perform amongst the myriad of studies that could be performed.  For the assumptions of the study, DEC establishes assumptions based on available information about the NITS request including type of load to be served, size of load, location of load, operating characteristics of the load, etc.

For instance, after DEC had already performed system impact and facilities studies on a 945 MW NITS request for new network load to be served in York, South Carolina near DEC’s 2,310 MW Catawba Nuclear Station (“Project Cobra Load”), NERC issued (a) the Large Loads Task Force White Paper on Characteristics and Risks of Emerging Large Loads Large Loads which discussed power quality issues raised by large loads and (b) an Industry Recommendation on Large Load Interconnection, Study, Commissioning, and Operations to, among other things, “address the risks observed from the analyzed large load behavior.”  Informed by the NERC issuances, DEC then determined that it needed to perform additional studies – stability and power quality studies – on the Project Cobra Load.  DEC entered into a Large Load Stability and Power Quality Study Agreement with the customer which described the study scope as follows:

-- Stability risks such as those resulting from ride-through behavior, voltage stability, angular stability, resonance and oscillation.
-- More detailed load models for stability analysis 
-- Power system analysis using Electromagnetic Transient simulations 
-- Power quality risks such as harmonics and voltage fluctuations. 
-- Impact on synchronous generators and nearby Catawba Nuclear Station including but not limited to
Sub-Synchronous Torsional Interaction 
Sub-Synchronous Resonance 
-- Engineering analysis for system upgrades and cost/schedule 

Attachment A to the study agreement set forth the assumptions for the study as follows: (a) 100% of the 945 MW new network load will be assumed to be an artificial intelligence and machine learning data center and (b) 0% of the 945 MW new network load will be assumed to be an enterprise data center, managed services data center, colocation data center, cloud computing data center, or edge data center.
DEC filed the study agreement with the Commission and the Commission issued an order accepting the agreement, stating that “[w]e find the Agreement just and reasonable because it will allow Duke to conduct the study to meet its responsibility, as the transmission provider, to ensure continued reliability of the transmission system.”  DEC expects that it will continue to establish the scope and assumptions for each study of NITS requests as described above and based on various attributes of the request which include MW size, location of new/modified load to other loads or generators on the system, operating characteristics of the load, etc.
DEC explains that, under proposed section I.1 of Attachment F to DEC’s pro forma NITSA, and section 4.5 of the PMPA NITSA, the Transmission Customer may not increase or decrease the MW value associated with the Network Load after Network Upgrades are identified.  Footnote 5 of proposed section I.1 of Attachment F to DEC’s pro forma NITSA states that the Transmission Customer must submit a new request to add additional new Network Load. 
Proposed section I.1 of Attachment F to DEC’s pro forma NITSA applies to all NITS requests, regardless of the size of the Network Load.  Please explain why this is appropriate for requests for NITS associated with all Network Load, as opposed to applying section I.1 solely to loads of 100 MW or greater.
Response: This section applies to a particular NITS request and does not prohibit customers from submitting successive requests over time to increase Network Load or decrease Network Load to be served by NITS.  For example, a customer may submit a NITS request for 10 MW, then for 100 MW then for 5 MW, then for 30 MW, and may submit such requests any time it wishes – days, weeks, months or years apart – and for any requested in-service dates that they choose.  This section does, however, contain a customer commitment that the customer will not seek to increase or decrease any particular NITS request once Network Upgrades have been identified.  This is appropriate for requests for NITS associated with all Network Load (not just loads of 100 MW or greater) because the Transmission Customer has requested a particular MW amount of Network Load to be served by NITS by a particular requested in-service date.  The Transmission Customer has 100% discretion and control to choose when to submit the request and to select its desired MW amount and in-service date for the load.  After submitting a request and entering into the requisite study agreements with the customer, the Transmission Provider then performs studies as required, identifies Direct Assignment Facilities and Network Upgrades to accommodate the request, and such facilities and upgrades will be constructed to accommodate the Network Load.  Once the Network Upgrades have been identified, it is at this point in the process that it is appropriate that the Transmission Customer does not increase or decrease the MW value of its request because the overall increased/decreased amount (as well as the incremental increase or decrease compared to its original request) was not studied.  The study reports did not identify the appropriate Direct Assignment Facilities and Network Upgrades for the increased or decreased MW value.  The studies were specific to the MW requested, and the necessary facilities and upgrades to the Transmission Provider’s system was sized accordingly.
DEC explained on page 22 of the transmittal letter submitted in this proceeding why this language is appropriate, which is appropriate for all NITS requests and not just those for 100 MW or greater loads:
“The customer commitment discussed above is necessary from an operational and rate recovery perspective.  From an operational perspective, the commitment in part (a) is necessary to ensure that all Network Upgrades necessary to accommodate the Network Load are completed prior to MWs of such Load coming online to ensure the system is prepared to handle those MWs in a safe and reliable manner necessary for smooth operation of the integrated networked transmission system.  Also from an operational perspective, the commitment in parts (b) and (c) are necessary because the identified Network Upgrades to accommodate the Network Load were sized to meet the needs of the MWs identified in the load schedule.  Adding MWs to the Network Load after those upgrades were identified would pose risks from an operational perspective that the additional MWs were not studied and the identified upgrades may be insufficient to accommodate the additional MWs.  If a Transmission Customer attempts to decrease its MWs of Network Load from what was studied and what the Transmission Provider is building to accommodate, this risks shifting costs to other customers.  From a rate recovery perspective, the costs of Network Upgrades will be rolled into transmission rate as prudent and reasonable investments in the transmission system to accommodate Network Load and paid for by customers according to their load ratio share.  Permitting decreases to a Transmission Customers’ studied new Network Load risks cost shifts to other customers and undermines the analysis performed to appropriately size required Network Upgrades to the requested new Network Load.”
DEC modeled its language pertaining to customer commitments to refrain from increasing or decreasing the MW amount of load to be studied by a certain time in the process on similar language in the eleven PECO, ComEd and Dayton agreements cited in the transmittal letter submitted in this proceeding, all of which were accepted by the Commission without modification.  DEC’s language is substantially the same as the language in these eleven cases and it is likewise just reasonable for customers to refrain from increasing or decreasing the MW amount of load that the customers themselves self-identified in a particular NITS request in order to (a) ensure Direct Assignment Facilities and Network Upgrades are truly needed and sized correctly to reliably serve the amount of load requested and (b) avoid the potential cost shifts to other customers that would arise if the system gets “overbuilt” to accommodate a NITS request that is later decreased in MW amount.  
Please explain the consequences of a Transmission Customer taking more or less service than the MW value associated with the Network Load, where the load is less than 100 MW.
Response:  The response below explains the consequences of a Transmission Customer taking more or less service than the MW value associated with the Network Load, where the load is less than 100 MW.
More Service:  The consequences of a Transmission Customer taking more service than the MW value are that (a) Transmission Provider did not have the opportunity to study the increased amount of service, (b) the Direct Assignment Facilities and Network Upgrades identified in studies for the original amount of service were sized to accommodate service at the requested MW amount (not the increased amount), (c) reliability of the system could be compromised or in jeopardy because more MWs are flowing onto the system through equipment that was not designed to accommodate the higher MW flow, and (d) ratepayers may have paid for transmission assets that were not sufficient to accommodate service and later were removed the system.
The following hypothetical example illustrates the consequences of a Transmission Customer taking more service than the MW value.  A NITS customer submits a transmission service request for 45 MW of new Network Load to be served at a new Delivery Point to be located on a 100 kV transmission line.  The Transmission Provider’s studies determine that a gang-operated air break (“GOAB”) switch needs to be installed to serve the new Delivery Point and costs $3 million.  After the GOAB is installed and the Transmission Provider begins providing NITS to the customer through the new Delivery Point, the NITS customer thereafter increases their use of NITS at this Delivery Point to 60 MW.  At this MW level, the GOAB switch is likely insufficient from a reliability perspective because the load is at too high a level to be reliably served from a single GOAB switch as the Delivery Point.  Had the Transmission Provider studied the requested new Network Load at 60 MW instead of 45 MW, the study would likely have determined that a new switching station that costs $30 million would be required to establish a new Point of Delivery to reliably serve the new Network Load.  At this point, the Transmission Provider would need to inform the NITS customer of the need to conduct a new study to determine what additional Direct Assignment Facilities or Network Upgrades would be needed to continue to reliably serve the 60 MW which is 15 MW greater than the request that was originally studied.  The NITS customer and Transmission Provider would need to enter into a new study agreement, the Transmission Provider would conduct the study at the NITS customer’s expense and provide the report to such customer.  In this hypothetical scenario, the Transmission Provider determines that a brand-new $3 million GOAB switch must be removed and a $30 million switching station must be constructed.  The Transmission Provider would post the study report on OASIS and the NITS customer and Transmission Provider would need to enter into an amended NITSA to memorialize the additional 15 MW of NITS to be provided to the customer.  The $3 million GOAB that was installed, included in transmission ratebase, and later removed from the system evidences the negative financial consequences to ratepayers of having paid their pro rata share of transmission assets that ultimately were not the correct assets necessary to accommodate service.  
Less Service:  The consequences of a Transmission Customer taking less service than the MW value are that (a) Transmission Provider did not have the opportunity to study the decreased amount of service, (b) the Direct Assignment Facilities and Network Upgrades identified in studies for the original amount of service were sized to accommodate service at the requested MW amount (not the decreased amount), (c) the transmission system was likely “overbuilt” to accommodate the original amount of MWs identified in the request and not the decreased amount, and (d) ratepayers may have paid for transmission assets that were not needed to accommodate lower service or they may have paid for more expensive modifications to the system to accommodate higher service than were actually needed to accommodate lower service.
The following hypothetical example illustrates the consequences of a Transmission Customer taking less service than the MW value.  A NITS customer submits a transmission service request for 10 MW of new Network Load to serve a new industrial load at an existing Point of Delivery located on a 44 kV transmission line.  The Transmission Provider’s studies determines that the 44 kV transmission line does not have sufficient capacity to reliably serve the additional 10 MW of load, and determines that a new 5-mile long 100 kV transmission line would need to be built, along with a new customer substation, to reliably serve the new 10 MW of load.  The new transmission line costs $10 million and the new customer substation costs $20 million.  After the new line and customer substation are installed and the Transmission Provider begins providing NITS to the customer, the NITS customer thereafter decreases their use of NITS to 4 MW.  At this MW level, it is likely that the existing 44 kV transmission line was adequate to serve load at this lower level and that the new 100 kV transmission line and customer substation was not required to accommodate service at this level.  The $30 million worth of Network Upgrades (the new $10 million 100 kV transmission line and $20 million new customer substation) that were installed and included in transmission rate base evidences the negative financial consequences to ratepayers of having paid their pro rata share to “overbuild” the transmission system to a degree that was not necessary to accommodate the lower amount of service actually taken.

REQUESTED EFFECTIVE DATE
DEC had sought an effective date of August 1, 2026 for the PMPA NITSA.  However, the Acting Director stated in the letter that “[t]he information requested in this letter order will constitute an amendment to your filing and a new filing date will be established.”
DEC renews its request for an effective date of August 1, 2026 because the Commission permits applicants to retain their original requested effective date when a filing is amended in good faith to cure a deficiency.  The initial filings in this docket and this deficiency letter response filing have been submitted in good faith, so all provide the same notice as to the timing under which the PMPA NITSA will become effective.

CONCLUSION
For the reasons above, DEC requests that the Commission (a) accept these responses to the letter and (b) issue an order accepting the PMPA NITSA for filing as of the requested effective date.  Please contact the undersigned if you have any questions.

                       SERVICE AGREEMENT FOR
             NETWORK INTEGRATION TRANSMISSION SERVICE

1.0   PARTIES

      This Service Agreement, dated as of August 1, 2026 is entered into, by and between
      Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC (“Transmission Provider”) and Piedmont Municipal
      Power Agency (“Transmission Customer”) sometimes hereinafter referred to
      individually as “Party” and collectively as “Parties”.

2.0   COMPLETED APPLICATION

      The Transmission Customer has been determined to have a Completed Application
      for Network Integration Transmission Service under Transmission Provider’s Open
      Access Transmission Tariff (the “Tariff”).

      If the corporate identity or name of Transmission Customer is to change during the
      term of this Service Agreement, Transmission Customer shall notify Transmission
      Provider as soon as possible after learning of said projected change. In such event
      Transmission Provider may in its reasonable discretion require a new Application for
      Network Integration Transmission Service and/or the execution of an appropriate
      amendment of this Service Agreement.

3.0   TERM

      Unless the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”)
      orders a different date for commencement of service, service under this Service
      Agreement shall commence on August 1, 2026 and continue to January 1, 2042.

4.0   EFFECT OF ISO/RTO PARTICIPATION

      This Service Agreement and the Attachments thereto (collectively, the “Service
      Agreement” or “Agreement”), have been developed by the Parties in the context of
      transmission service provided pursuant to the Tariff and the Commission’s open
      access requirements under Order No. 888 and Order No. 890. Were the Transmission
      Provider to join a Regional Transmission Organization (“RTO”) (which term includes
      an independent system operator), the Transmission Provider is permitted to assign
      this service agreement to the RTO, in which case transmission service would be
      provided to the Transmission Customer pursuant to the rates, terms and conditions of
      the open access transmission tariff of the RTO (“RTO OATT”), and other terms,
      conditions, rules and/or protocols of the RTO. The Parties further agree that in the
      event of a material inconsistency or conflict between the RTO OATT or such other
      terms, conditions, rules and/or protocols of the RTO and the Service Agreement, that
      the Service Agreement may require amendment to account for such changed
      circumstance. In such event, at the request of either Party or the RTO, the
      Transmission Customer and the RTO (and the Transmission Provider, if appropriate)


                                       Page 1
       shall enter into good faith negotiations to amend the Service Agreement in a manner
      such that the transmission service is provided in accordance with the RTO OATT and
      such other terms, conditions, rules and/or protocols. If the Transmission Customer
      and the RTO (and the Transmission Provider if appropriate) cannot agree on the
      necessary revisions the Transmission Customer may request that the RTO (and the
      Transmission Provider, if appropriate) file unexecuted amended Service Agreement
      with the Commission pursuant to Section 205 of the Federal Power Act such that the
      transmission service thereunder comports with the RTO OATT and such other terms,
      conditions rules and/or protocols of the RTO and the Transmission Provider shall
      support the Transmission Customer’s right to request such filing. By agreeing to the
      procedure set forth above, neither Party waives any rights it might otherwise have
      with respect to the Service Agreement under the Federal Power Act.

5.0   NATURE OF SERVICE TO BE FURNISHED

      The Transmission Provider agrees to provide, and the Transmission Customer agrees
      to take and pay, for Network Integration Transmission Service in accordance with the
      provisions of Part III of the Tariff and this Service Agreement as they may be
      amended from time to time. Neither Party shall be deemed, by virtue of having
      entered into this Service Agreement, to have agreed to diminish or enhance the rights
      of either Party with regard to the Commission’s comparability policies, provided that
      the foregoing clause shall be construed in a manner most consistent with each Party
      performing its obligations hereunder.

7.0   INCORPORATION OF OTHER DOCUMENTS

      The Tariff, Attachment A hereto (Specifications for Network Integration
      Transmission Service), Attachment B hereto (Delivery Points), Attachment C hereto
      (Distribution Rates), Attachment D hereto (Power Factor Penalty), Attachment E
      hereto (Network Operating Agreement), and Attachment F hereto (Other
      Charges/Credits) are incorporated herein and made a part hereof.

      To the extent that any provisions in the Tariff or this Service Agreement are
      ambiguous or inconsistent, any such ambiguity or inconsistency will be resolved in
      the following priority: the Tariff, the Service Agreement (including Attachments).

8.0   BILLINGS AND BILLING ADJUSTMENTS

      8.1   The Transmission Provider will have the right to adjust or revise any bill
            rendered under the Tariff no later than eighteen (18) months after the date the
            bill was rendered. Any billing adjustment will be in writing and will state the
            specific basis for the adjustment. An Adjusted Bill will constitute a new bill in
            regard to the adjusted components for all purposes of the Tariff and this Service
            Agreement.

      8.2   The Transmission Customer may, in good faith, challenge the correctness of any
            bill and any adjusted or revised bills. The Transmission Customer’s challenge
            of any bill rendered under the Tariff may include the appropriateness of all
            charges thereunder. Unless otherwise agreed in writing by the Parties, the
            Transmission Customer’s challenge must be presented no later than eighteen
            (18) months following the date such bill is received. Any billing challenge will
            be in writing and will state the specific basis for the challenge. Billing
            challenges are limited in scope to the correctness of any bill and appropriateness
            of any charge. The Transmission Provider shall respond in writing to any such
            billing challenge within ninety (90) days. Billing challenges shall be treated as
            disputes pursuant to Section 7.3 of the Tariff.

      8.3   Refunds or additional charges that are a result of an adjustment, revision, or
            billing challenge will include interest calculated at the rate set forth in 18 C.F.R.
            § 35.19a (a)(2)(iii).

9.0   AUDITS

      9.1   In addition to the bill challenge rights set forth in Section 8.2, the Transmission
            Customer shall also have audit rights as set forth in this Section 9.0. The
            Transmission Customer shall conduct any such audit within eighteen (18)
            months from the date of the rendering of any bill under the Tariff. The
            Transmission Provider and the Transmission Customer will each have the right,
            upon reasonable notice, to inspect or audit each other’s accounts and records
            supporting the bills for service under the Tariff during such calendar year. Such


                                          Page 3
              audit will be performed to the extent necessary to verify the correctness of any
             bill and the appropriateness of all charges thereunder. The audited Party shall
             provide or cause to be provided all information that the auditing Party may
             reasonably request to substantiate all billings, adjustments or revisions to
             billings for service under the Tariff. Any such audit will be conducted, upon
             reasonable written notice, during normal business hours at the offices where
             such accounts and records are maintained or at a location mutually agreeable to
             the Parties. The audited Party shall provide to the auditing Party reasonable
             office accommodations to conduct the audit. Those qualified personnel
             identified upon reasonable written notice by the auditing Party will be permitted
             to conduct audits. The audited Party will be entitled to review the audit report
             and any supporting materials at the conclusion of the audit and prior to
             finalization. The accounts and records for any calendar year shall not be subject
             to more than one (1) audit by a Party.

       9.2   Notwithstanding the above, if the Transmission Provider renders a billing
             adjustment or revision and the audit for the affected calendar year has been
             conducted, then the Transmission Customer may conduct an audit of the billing
             adjustment or revision within ninety (90) days after the adjustment is rendered
             and challenge such adjustment no later than one hundred and fifty (150) days
             after the adjustment is rendered.

       9.3   With the exception of quantifiable changes in the amounts of the billings, the
             audit report, supporting materials and all other audit results of all such audits
             shall be kept confidential by the Parties and shall not be released to any other
             party without the express written consent of the other Party.

10.0   DELIVERY POINTS

       The Transmission Customer Delivery Points shall be the points of connection
       between the Transmission Provider’s facilities and the facilities of the Transmission
       Customer or its member systems.

11.0   ADJUSTMENT FOR LOSSES

       To the extent any Delivery Point is at a voltage level less than 44 kV or the metering
       point(s) is (are) remote from the Delivery Point, the load associated with such
       Delivery Point used for the calculation of the Network Integration Transmission
       Service charge shall be adjusted for the losses associated with: (i) the Transmission
       Provider’s applicable distribution facilities; and/or (ii) the Transmission Customer’s
       distribution and transmission facilities, as applicable. Such loss compensation factors
       shall be as mutually agreed upon by the Parties. To the extent the Parties cannot




                                          Page 4
        agree on any such factors, the Dispute Resolution Procedures in Section 12 of the
       Tariff may be invoked to resolve the disagreement.

12.0   NO WAIVERS

       Failure of a Party to enforce any provision of this Service Agreement will not be
       construed as a waiver of such provision, and will not affect the validity of the Service
       Agreement or the right of either Party subsequently to enforce any provision of the
       Service Agreement. Any waiver at any time by either Party of its rights with respect
       to the other Party, or with respect to any matter arising in connection with this Service
       Agreement, will not be considered a waiver with respect to any subsequent matter.
       Failure of a Party to resort to any legal remedy or to exercise any one or more
       alternative remedies will not affect such Party’s right subsequently to resort to any
       one or more of such rights or remedies on account of any such grounds then existing,
       or which may subsequently occur.

13.0   ACCEPTANCE BY FERC

       The Parties recognize that this Service Agreement must be filed with the FERC and is
       subject to the jurisdiction of that Commission. Transmission Provider shall have the
       right to make a unilateral filing with the Commission to modify this Service
       Agreement with respect to any rates, terms and conditions, charges, classifications of
       service, rule or regulation under section 205 or any other applicable provision of the
       Federal Power Act and the Commission’s rules and regulations thereunder, and
       Transmission Customer shall have the right to make a unilateral filing with the
       Commission to modify this Service Agreement pursuant to section 206 or any other
       applicable provision of the Federal Power Act and FERC’s rules and regulations
       thereunder; provided that each Party shall have the right to protest any such filing by
       the other Party and to participate fully in any proceeding before FERC in which such
       modifications may be considered. Nothing in this Service Agreement shall limit the
       rights of the Parties or of the Commission under sections 205 or 206 of the Federal
       Power Act and FERC’s rules and regulations thereunder, except to the extent that the
       Parties otherwise mutually agree as provided herein.

4.0   Network Load

      The Network Load is the demand and energy requirement for the member systems of
      Transmission Customer at the Delivery Points connected to the Transmission
      Provider’s transmission and distribution system, as set forth in Attachment B, as may
      be amended from time to time.

      4.1         Transmission Customer’s load growth shall not be treated as ‘New Network
                  Load’ pursuant to Section 31.2 of the Transmission Provider’s Tariff.
                  Transmission Customer estimated load growth shall be reflected in the annual
                  updates of forecasted Network Load provided pursuant to Section 31.6 of the
                  Transmission Provider’s Tariff.

 4.2   For purposes of calculating the Transmission Customer’s load ratio share of
      the transmission system revenue requirement, load served by generating
      resources that utilize the transmission or distribution facilities of a
      Transmission Customer Participant to reach load (“behind-the-meter
      generation”) shall be included in the Transmission Customer’s Network Load
      to the extent permitted by FERC policy, provided, however, that if FERC’s
      policy with respect to the treatment of load served by ‘behind-the-meter
      generation’ is modified, the treatment accorded Transmission Customer load
      served by such generation shall be conformed to FERC’s modified treatment.

4.3   For purposes of calculating the Transmission Customer’s load ratio share of
      the transmission system revenue requirement, Network Load shall not include
      load served by generating resources located “behind the second meter” that is
      unknown to the Transmission Customer (i.e., generation that does not utilize
      the transmission or distribution system of a wholesale transmission customer
      to reach load or does not operate in synchronization with the Transmission
      Provider’s transmission system), provided, however, that the calculation of

      if: (i) FERC rules in a contested proceeding that load served by generation
      located behind the second meter must be included in a Transmission

a. System Impact Studies and Facilities Studies Conducted by

    the cost of any required Network Upgrades, and (iii) the time required to

   The Facilities Study report dated March 20, 2026 contained each of the
   required 3 elements as set forth below.

   Good Faith Estimate of Cost of Direct Assignment Facilities: there
   were no direct assignment facilities identified in the study to be charged
   to the Transmission Customer.

   Good Faith Estimate of Cost of Any Required Network Upgrades:
   the study report contained Transmission Provider’s good faith estimate of
   the following transmission Network Upgrades are needed to serve this
   new network load: (1) Install new remote controlled Gang Operated Air-
   break Switch on existing Transmission Customer Delivery Tap line at
   structure number 24.5.

   Transmission Provider provided a good faith estimate of the cost of such
   updates as approximately $3.35 million which is comprised of the
   following components: (1) costs to engineer and design the removal of
   existing structure and the installation of new structure with Gang
   Operated Air-break Switch at structure 24.5, (2) material costs to source
   and procure all necessary equipment based on historical pricing of
   procuring similar equipment in the past, estimates of quantities of
   equipment needed in this case, and quotes from vendors on such material
   costs, (3) construction costs to construct and install the Network
   Upgrades which includes direct charges for subcontracted labor to do so
   based upon scope of work for the Network Upgrades and existing labor
   rates, (4) indirect charges to produce a fully burden cost estimate
   including material loading and allocation values, overhead costs,
   administrative expenses, and escalator calculations to account for any
   cost increases based on standard methodologies employed by
   Transmission Provider in creating good faith cost estimates, and (5) a
   contingency reserve amount to cover unforeseen expenditures established
   as a percentage of overall direct and indirect costs (20%) which is
   aligned with the standard project management governance requirements
   employed by Transmission Provider in creating good faith cost estimates.

   Good Faith Estimate of Time Required to Complete Such
   Construction and Initiate the Requested Service: the study report
   contained Transmission Provider’s good faith estimate of 30 months to
   complete construction of Network Upgrades.

   cancel or delay a requested change in Network Integration Transmission

   new Network Load) in any way relieve the Network Customer of its
   obligation to pay the costs of transmission facilities constructed by the
   Transmission Provider and charged to the Network Customer as reflected
   in the Service Agreement.”

   In the case of a cancellation or delay of this new Network Load, (1) costs

   incurs in returning the Transmission System to a safe and reliable
   condition (if any) will be charged to the Transmission Customer.

   Payment During Dispute. In the event of a billing dispute among the

   continues to make all payments not in dispute; and (2) pays to

   Transmission Customer fails to meet these two requirements, then
   Transmission Provider may provide notice to Transmission Customer of
   a Default pursuant to Breach, Cure and Default section. Within thirty

   money to another Party shall pay the amount due with interest calculated

of measurement and the Delivery Point will be agreed upon in writing between the

used in billing and accounting hereunder will in all cases include adjustments for such

6.0   Control Area and Data Equipment

      (a)    The Transmission Customer will be responsible for the purchase, installation,

      Provider’s Control Area, provided that such standards and practices are applied by the
      Transmission Provider on a consistent and non-discriminatory basis to all Transmission

 Customers. Prior to its installation, the Transmission Provider and the Transmission

conformance with such standards or practices.

(b)      The real time telemetry and data to be received by the Transmission Provider’s
system operator and the Transmission Customer shall be determined initially by the
Parties. Subsequent changes shall be determined by the Network Operating Committee.
Such telemetry and data shall be necessary for monitoring of system operations for
reliability, security or economics. Such telemetry may include but is not limited to loads,
line flows, voltages, and breaker status at any of the Transmission Customer’s
transmission facilities, and Transmission Customer owned generator output. All such
determinations under this subsection (b) shall be in accordance with Good Utility
Practice. To the extent telemetry is required that is not available on the Transmission
Customer’s facilities, the Transmission Customer, at its own expense, shall install any
metering equipment, data acquisition equipment, or other equipment and software on its
system that is necessary for the telemetry to be received by the Transmission Provider’s
system operator.

(c)   Each party shall be responsible for implementing any computer modifications or
changes required to its own computer system(s) as necessary to implement this Section.

(d)     The Transmission Customer will be responsible for the provision of scheduling
information (including the calculation of any dynamic information used for scheduling
and for any real-time modification of such dynamic scheduling information) necessary to
coordinate the Transmission Customer’s supply of energy from Network Resources and
non-designated Network Resources which may be scheduled from time to time to serve a
portion of the Transmission Customer’s Network Load.

(e)     To the extent that data required to determine the scheduling information pursuant

inaccurate, the Transmission Customer may use reasonable procedures, consistent with
Good Utility Practice, to estimate such unavailable or inaccurate data.

(f)    The dynamic scheduling arrangements will be deemed to be in a state of
successful operation if the dynamic scheduling information necessary for system
operations is being made available to the Transmission Provider and other entities as
required by agreement of the Parties (‘Successful Operation’). The Parties agree that

dynamic scheduling information being one hundred percent (100%) accurate. The
Parties agree, however, that so long as the dynamic scheduling arrangements yield

Parties to be adequate for continuing operational purposes, the state of Successful

7.0   Operating Requirements

      (a)     The Transmission Customer shall operate, or cause to be operated, its generating

      required by NERC or SERC, or any of their successors and consistently adhered to by the
      Transmission Provider.

      (b)      Insofar as practicable, the Transmission Provider and the Transmission Customer
      shall protect, operate, and maintain their respective systems so as to avoid or minimize
      the likelihood of disturbances which might cause impairment of service on the system(s)
      of the other. The Parties, consistent with Good Utility Practice, shall implement load
      shedding programs to maintain the reliability and integrity of the Transmission System,
      as provided in Section 33.6 of the Tariff. Load shedding shall include automatic load
      shedding by underfrequency relay or manual load shedding. The Transmission Provider
      will implement load shedding to maintain the relative sizes of load served by the affected
      facilities, unless otherwise required by circumstances beyond the control of the
      Transmission Provider or the Transmission Customer. Automatic load shedding devices
      will operate without notice. When manual load shedding is relied upon, the Transmission
      Provider shall notify the Transmission Customer’s dispatchers or schedulers of the
      required action and the Transmission Customer shall take immediate steps to comply.

      (c)     The Transmission Customer shall, at its own expense, provide, operate, and
      maintain in service high-speed, underfrequency load shedding equipment consistent with
      NERC and SERC, or any of their successor’s requirements. The Transmission Customer

      percent (30%) of its Network Load in a manner consistent with that followed by the
      Transmission Provider, which is three steps of approximately ten percent (10%) each at

      purposes of automatic load shedding, the Transmission Customer’s Network Load is
      covered under the Transmission Provider’s existing underfrequency relay systems. At

      are necessary. The installation on the Transmission Customer’s facilities of
      underfrequency relays to accomplish any additional load shedding above that already
      installed shall be completed on a schedule agreed to by the Network Operating
      Committee. The Network Operating Committee may review the amount of load that

8.0   Operational Information

      (a)     The Transmission Customer shall provide by September 1 of each year the
      Transmission Customer’s Network Resource availability forecast (e.g., all planned
      resource outages, including off-line and on-line dates) for the following year. Such

      Customer shall inform the Transmission Provider, in a timely manner, of any changes to
      the Transmission Customer’s Network Resource availability forecast. In the event that
      the Transmission Provider determines, in compliance with its rights and responsibilities
      under the Tariff, that such forecast changes cannot be accommodated due to a
      transmission constraint on its Transmission System, then the Transmission Provider shall
      notify the Network Operating Committee which shall meet to resolve the matter. If the
      Network Operating Committee is unable to resolve the matter in a timely fashion, then
      the Dispute Resolution Procedures set forth in Section 12 of the Tariff shall apply.

      (b)    The Transmission Customer shall provide, at least thirty-six (36) hours in advance
      of every calendar day, the Transmission Customer’s best forecast of any planned
      transmission or Network Resource outage(s) and other operating information reasonably
      required by the Transmission Provider to provide Transmission Service under the Service
      Agreement. In the event that such planned outages cannot be accommodated due to a
      transmission constraint on the Transmission Provider’s Transmission System and the
      Network Operating Committee cannot agree on remedial measures, the provisions of
      Section 33 of the Tariff will be implemented.

      (c)    The Transmission Provider and the Transmission Customer shall notify and
      coordinate with the other Party prior to the commencement of any work by either Party

      (d)     All information provided by either Party to the other under this Section shall be

 9.0    Network Planning

       Load and Network Resources, as well as any other information reasonably necessary for
       the Transmission Provider to plan for Network Integration Transmission Service. This
       type of information is consistent with the Transmission Provider’s information
       requirements for planning to serve its Native Load Customers. The data will be provided
       in a format consistent with that used by the Transmission Provider.

11.0   Character of Service

       Power and energy delivered under the Service Agreement shall be delivered as three-
       phase alternating current at a frequency of approximately 60 Hertz, and at the nominal
       voltages at the Delivery and Receipt points.

12.0   Transfer of Power and Energy Through Other Systems

       Since the Transmission Provider’s Transmission System is, and will be, directly and
       indirectly connected with other electric systems, it is recognized that, because of the
       physical and electrical characteristics of the facilities involved, power delivered under the
       Service Agreement will flow through such other systems. The Parties agree to advise
       other electric systems as deemed appropriate of such scheduled transfers and to attempt
       to maintain good relationships with affected third parties. The Parties further agree that
       the Transmission Customer or its duly appointed agent, will be responsible for making
       appropriate arrangements, consistent with the Tariff, for: (i) the scheduling and delivery

       Southern Company Control Area to the Transmission Provider’s Control Area; and (ii)
       any other transmission provider as necessary for the scheduling and delivery of power
       and energy from any other designated or non-designated Network Resources of the
       Transmission Customer to the Transmission Provider’s Control Area.

1.0   PARTIES

      This Service Agreement, dated as of JanuaryAugust 1, 20252026 is entered into, by
      and between Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC (“Transmission Provider”) and
      Piedmont Municipal Power Agency (“Transmission Customer”) sometimes
      hereinafter referred to individually as “Party” and collectively as “Parties”.

2.0   COMPLETED APPLICATION

      The Transmission Customer has been determined to have a Completed Application
      for Network Integration Transmission Service under Transmission Provider’s Open
      Access Transmission Tariff (the “Tariff”).

      If the corporate identity or name of Transmission Customer is to change during the
      term of this Service Agreement, Transmission Customer shall notify Transmission
      Provider as soon as possible after learning of said projected change. In such event
      Transmission Provider may in its reasonable discretion require a new Application for
      Network Integration Transmission Service and/or the execution of an appropriate
      amendment of this Service Agreement.

3.0   TERM

      Unless the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”)
      orders a different date for commencement of service, service under this Service
      Agreement shall commence on the later of: (1) the date the conditions precedent to
      receiving service set forth in Section 29.1 of the Tariff are met: or (2) January 1,
      2025. Unless terminated pursuant to the provisions hereof, service under this Service
      Agreement shall continue to January 1, 2033. If the Service Agreement is not
      terminated by the Transmission Provider or the Transmission Customer, the Service
      Agreement will automatically renew for successive five year terms. The Service
      Agreement may be terminated at the end of each successive five year term by the
      Transmission Provider or the Transmission Customer by giving notice of such
      termination in writing at least one year prior to the end of the renewal period.August
      1, 2026 and continue to January 1, 2042.

4.0   EFFECT OF ISO/RTO PARTICIPATION

      This Service Agreement and the Attachments thereto (collectively, the “Service
      Agreement” or “Agreement”), have been developed by the Parties in the context of
      transmission service provided pursuant to the Tariff and the Commission’s open
      access requirements under Order No. 888 and Order No. 890. Were the Transmission
      Provider to join a Regional Transmission Organization (“RTO”) (which term includes
      an independent system operator), the Transmission Provider is permitted to assign


                                        Page 1
       this service agreement to the RTO, in which case transmission service would be
      provided to the Transmission Customer pursuant to the rates, terms and conditions of
      the open access transmission tariff of the RTO (“RTO OATT”), and other terms,
      conditions, rules and/or protocols of the RTO. The Parties further agree that in the
      event of a material inconsistency or conflict between the RTO OATT or such other
      terms, conditions, rules and/or protocols of the RTO and the Service Agreement, that
      the Service Agreement may require amendment to account for such changed
      circumstance. In such event, at the request of either Party or the RTO, the
      Transmission Customer and the RTO (and the Transmission Provider, if appropriate)
      shall enter into good faith negotiations to amend the Service Agreement in a manner
      such that the transmission service is provided in accordance with the RTO OATT and
      such other terms, conditions, rules and/or protocols. If the Transmission Customer
      and the RTO (and the Transmission Provider if appropriate) cannot agree on the
      necessary revisions the Transmission Customer may request that the RTO (and the
      Transmission Provider, if appropriate) file unexecuted amended Service Agreement
      with the Commission pursuant to Section 205 of the Federal Power Act such that the
      transmission service thereunder comports with the RTO OATT and such other terms,
      conditions rules and/or protocols of the RTO and the Transmission Provider shall
      support the Transmission Customer’s right to request such filing. By agreeing to the
      procedure set forth above, neither Party waives any rights it might otherwise have
      with respect to the Service Agreement under the Federal Power Act.

5.0   NATURE OF SERVICE TO BE FURNISHED

      The Transmission Provider agrees to provide, and the Transmission Customer agrees
      to take and pay, for Network Integration Transmission Service in accordance with the
      provisions of Part III of the Tariff and this Service Agreement as they may be
      amended from time to time. Neither Party shall be deemed, by virtue of having
      entered into this Service Agreement, to have agreed to diminish or enhance the rights
      of either Party with regard to the Commission’s comparability policies, provided that
      the foregoing clause shall be construed in a manner most consistent with each Party
      performing its obligations hereunder.

      To the extent that any provisions in the Tariff or this Service Agreement are
      ambiguous or inconsistent, any such ambiguity or inconsistency will be resolved in
      the following priority: the Tariff, the Service Agreement (including Attachments).

8.0   BILLINGS AND BILLING ADJUSTMENTS

      8.1   The Transmission Provider will have the right to adjust or revise any bill
            rendered under the Tariff no later than eighteen (18) months after the date the
            bill was rendered. Any billing adjustment will be in writing and will state the
            specific basis for the adjustment. An Adjusted Bill will constitute a new bill in
            regard to the adjusted components for all purposes of the Tariff and this Service
            Agreement.

      8.2   The Transmission Customer may, in good faith, challenge the correctness of any
            bill and any adjusted or revised bills. The Transmission Customer’s challenge
            of any bill rendered under the Tariff may include the appropriateness of all
            charges thereunder. Unless otherwise agreed in writing by the Parties, the
            Transmission Customer’s challenge must be presented no later than eighteen
            (18) months following the date such bill is received. Any billing challenge will
            be in writing and will state the specific basis for the challenge. Billing
            challenges are limited in scope to the correctness of any bill and appropriateness
            of any charge. The Transmission Provider shall respond in writing to any such
            billing challenge within ninety (90) days. Billing challenges shall be treated as
            disputes pursuant to Section 7.3 of the Tariff.

      8.3   Refunds or additional charges that are a result of an adjustment, revision, or
            billing challenge will include interest calculated at the rate set forth in 18 C.F.R.
            § 35.19a (a)(2)(iii).

 9.0    AUDITS

       9.1   In addition to the bill challenge rights set forth in Section 8.2, the Transmission
             Customer shall also have audit rights as set forth in this Section 9.0. The
             Transmission Customer shall conduct any such audit within eighteen (18)
             months from the date of the rendering of any bill under the Tariff. The
             Transmission Provider and the Transmission Customer will each have the right,
             upon reasonable notice, to inspect or audit each other’s accounts and records
             supporting the bills for service under the Tariff during such calendar year. Such
             audit will be performed to the extent necessary to verify the correctness of any
             bill and the appropriateness of all charges thereunder. The audited Party shall
             provide or cause to be provided all information that the auditing Party may
             reasonably request to substantiate all billings, adjustments or revisions to
             billings for service under the Tariff. Any such audit will be conducted, upon
             reasonable written notice, during normal business hours at the offices where
             such accounts and records are maintained or at a location mutually agreeable to
             the Parties. The audited Party shall provide to the auditing Party reasonable
             office accommodations to conduct the audit. Those qualified personnel
             identified upon reasonable written notice by the auditing Party will be permitted
             to conduct audits. The audited Party will be entitled to review the audit report
             and any supporting materials at the conclusion of the audit and prior to
             finalization. The accounts and records for any calendar year shall not be subject
             to more than one (1) audit by a Party.

       9.2   Notwithstanding the above, if the Transmission Provider renders a billing
             adjustment or revision and the audit for the affected calendar year has been
             conducted, then the Transmission Customer may conduct an audit of the billing
             adjustment or revision within ninety (90) days after the adjustment is rendered
             and challenge such adjustment no later than one hundred and fifty (150) days
             after the adjustment is rendered.

             audit report, supporting materials and all other audit results of all such audits
             shall be kept confidential by the Parties and shall not be released to any other
             party without the express written consent of the other Party.

       Delivery Point used for the calculation of the Network Integration Transmission

       shall be as mutually agreed upon by the Parties. To the extent the Parties cannot
       agree on any such factors, the Dispute Resolution Procedures in Section 12 of the
       Tariff may be invoked to resolve the disagreement.

12.0   NO WAIVERS

       construed as a waiver of such provision, and will not affect the validity of the Service
       Agreement or the right of either Party subsequently to enforce any provision of the
       Service Agreement. Any waiver at any time by either Party of its rights with respect
       to the other Party, or with respect to any matter arising in connection with this Service
       Agreement, will not be considered a waiver with respect to any subsequent matter.
       Failure of a Party to resort to any legal remedy or to exercise any one or more
       alternative remedies will not affect such Party’s right subsequently to resort to any
       one or more of such rights or remedies on account of any such grounds then existing,
       or which may subsequently occur.

13.0   ACCEPTANCE BY FERC

       subject to the jurisdiction of that Commission. Transmission Provider shall have the
       right to make a unilateral filing with the Commission to modify this Service
       Agreement with respect to any rates, terms and conditions, charges, classifications of
       service, rule or regulation under section 205 or any other applicable provision of the
       Federal Power Act and the Commission’s rules and regulations thereunder, and
       Transmission Customer shall have the right to make a unilateral filing with the
       Commission to modify this Service Agreement pursuant to section 206 or any other
       applicable provision of the Federal Power Act and FERC’s rules and regulations
       thereunder; provided that each Party shall have the right to protest any such filing by

       rights of the Parties or of the Commission under sections 205 or 206 of the Federal
       Power Act and FERC’s rules and regulations thereunder, except to the extent that the

      This Service Agreement, dated as of August 1, 2026 is entered into, by and between
      Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC (“Transmission Provider”) and Piedmont Municipal
      Power Agency (“Transmission Customer”) sometimes hereinafter referred to
      individually as “Party” and collectively as “Parties”.

2.0   COMPLETED APPLICATION

      The Transmission Customer has been determined to have a Completed Application
      for Network Integration Transmission Service under Transmission Provider’s Open
      Access Transmission Tariff (the “Tariff”).

      If the corporate identity or name of Transmission Customer is to change during the
      term of this Service Agreement, Transmission Customer shall notify Transmission
      Provider as soon as possible after learning of said projected change. In such event
      Transmission Provider may in its reasonable discretion require a new Application for
      Network Integration Transmission Service and/or the execution of an appropriate
      amendment of this Service Agreement.

3.0   TERM

      orders a different date for commencement of service, service under this Service
      Agreement shall commence on August 1, 2026 and continue to January 1, 2042.

4.0   EFFECT OF ISO/RTO PARTICIPATION

      Agreement” or “Agreement”), have been developed by the Parties in the context of
      transmission service provided pursuant to the Tariff and the Commission’s open
      access requirements under Order No. 888 and Order No. 890. Were the Transmission
      Provider to join a Regional Transmission Organization (“RTO”) (which term includes
      an independent system operator), the Transmission Provider is permitted to assign
      this service agreement to the RTO, in which case transmission service would be
      provided to the Transmission Customer pursuant to the rates, terms and conditions of
      the open access transmission tariff of the RTO (“RTO OATT”), and other terms,
      conditions, rules and/or protocols of the RTO. The Parties further agree that in the
      event of a material inconsistency or conflict between the RTO OATT or such other
      terms, conditions, rules and/or protocols of the RTO and the Service Agreement, that
      the Service Agreement may require amendment to account for such changed
      circumstance. In such event, at the request of either Party or the RTO, the
      Transmission Customer and the RTO (and the Transmission Provider, if appropriate)

      such that the transmission service is provided in accordance with the RTO OATT and
      such other terms, conditions, rules and/or protocols. If the Transmission Customer

      necessary revisions the Transmission Customer may request that the RTO (and the
      Transmission Provider, if appropriate) file unexecuted amended Service Agreement

      transmission service thereunder comports with the RTO OATT and such other terms,
      conditions rules and/or protocols of the RTO and the Transmission Provider shall

      with respect to the Service Agreement under the Federal Power Act.

8.0   BILLINGS AND BILLING ADJUSTMENTS
